title: FRM Credit Risk, Lesson 3: Counterparty credit risk (CVA) and portfolio credit models
subtitle: Why a derivative contract that is worth money to you can still cost you money
whyItMatters: Credit risk does not sit only with the person who borrowed the cash. Any derivative contract - an interest rate swap, a forward, a CDS - carries the risk that the counterparty fails to perform at a moment when the contract is in your favour. CVA (Credit Valuation Adjustment) is how that cost is quantified precisely, and it is one of the capital charges Basel III requires banks to hold separately.
openingQuestion: What does CVA (Credit Valuation Adjustment) measure?
openingOptions: The capital needed to open a new bank branch in a high-risk region
The markdown of a derivative's value for counterparty risk
The average non-performing loan ratio of the banking sector over a financial year
The deposit insurance premium a bank pays into the deposit protection scheme
explanation: CVA is the market value of the derivative assuming no counterparty risk, less an adjustment for the possibility that the counterparty defaults. In substance it prices a simple question: if my counterparty defaults at a moment when the contract is in my favour, how much do I lose? The figure grows with the counterparty's probability of default and with the expected value of the contract.

diagram.label: Enter a derivative contract with a counterparty, an interest rate swap say
The contract's value moves with the market: sometimes positive, sometimes negative to you
The counterparty defaults at a moment when the contract is positive to you
You lose that value - CVA is the expected cost of exactly this risk

realWorldExample.description: When Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, thousands of derivative counterparties worldwide - mostly on interest rate swaps and CDS - suddenly had to deal with counterparty risk that had become real: contracts standing in their favour, where Lehman owed them money, turned into claims inside a bankruptcy process that ran for years and typically recovered a small fraction of face value. That episode is the direct reason Basel III wrote a CVA capital charge into the framework; before it, many banks held no dedicated capital against this risk at all.

quiz.question: Why does CVA arise only when a derivative contract is positive in value to you, and not when it is negative?
options: Because in practice a derivative contract is never negative in value to either side of the trade once collateral has been posted
Because Basel III forbids computing CVA on any derivative contract standing at negative value on the valuation date, whatever the product or the counterparty involved
Because CVA only applies to derivative contracts with a remaining maturity of under one year from the valuation date
Because if the contract is negative to you - you owe the counterparty - their default costs you nothing, since you still owe that money whether they survive or not
quiz.explanation: Counterparty risk runs in one direction only: a default hurts you only when the counterparty OWES you, which is to say when the contract stands in your favour. If you owe them, their failure does not release you from the obligation. That asymmetry is why CVA is computed on expected positive exposure rather than on the full contract value, and why maturity and product type are not what determines whether the charge applies.

quiz.question: Why was the Basel III CVA capital charge added to the framework?
options: Because the 2008 crisis, and Lehman Brothers above all, showed that banks were taking heavy losses on derivative counterparty risk against which no dedicated capital was held
Because supervisors wanted to raise more tax revenue out of the banking sector once the crisis had passed and bank profits had recovered
Because CVA replaces the ordinary credit capital requirements carried over from Basel II rather than sitting alongside them
Because the banks proposed the extra charge themselves in order to impress investors and the rating agencies, entirely without any pressure at all from the supervisory authorities
quiz.explanation: Before 2008, counterparty credit risk on the derivatives book largely sat outside the formal capital requirements. Lehman's collapse showed that this class of loss - CVA losses - could in many cases exceed the losses from outright default, which led Basel III to require capital against it explicitly. It supplements the Basel II credit charge rather than replacing it, and it arrived as a supervisory mandate rather than an industry initiative.

quiz.question: How does a portfolio credit risk model differ from assessing each loan on its own?
options: There is no difference of substance at all; the two approaches produce exactly the same answer once every individual loan in the book has been properly assessed
A portfolio model works only where every loan carries the same credit rating, and cannot be used at all once a book holds several different rating grades in one basket

A portfolio model accounts for default correlation between different loans and counterparties, because total portfolio loss depends on whether they tend to default together or independently of each other
A portfolio model ignores the individual probability of default on each of the loans entirely and looks only at the total size of the book that it covers
quiz.explanation: This is why credit correlation is both the most important and the hardest parameter to estimate in portfolio credit risk - and it is precisely what broke the CDO models before 2008, which understated how far loans can default together under a systemic shock. A portfolio model needs each individual probability of default as an input rather than discarding it, and mixed-rating books are the normal case it was built for.

quiz.question: If a counterparty's probability of default rises - a rating downgrade, say - what happens to the CVA on contracts standing in your favour?
options: CVA falls, because a riskier counterparty pays a lower fee as compensation
CVA is unchanged, since it depends only on the market value of the contract
CVA rises, because the risk of not collecting what they owe has gone up
CVA turns negative, converting the contract into a guaranteed profit line
quiz.explanation: CVA moves directly with the counterparty's probability of default: as counterparty risk rises, so does the expected cost of not collecting what they owe on a contract standing in your favour, which forces the bank to book a CVA loss even though no default event has yet taken place. Nothing about a fee schedule offsets that, the rating is an input rather than an irrelevance, and CVA is a cost that reduces value rather than one that can invert into a gain.

quiz.question: Why does the credit valuation adjustment arise only when the derivative is positive in value to you?
options: Because accounting standards require an adjustment on the asset side only
Because a contract with negative value is automatically terminated early
Because the side holding negative value posts no collateral to the other
Because only then are you the one holding a receivable if they default
quiz.explanation: A counterparty defaulting while they owe you money costs you; defaulting while you owe them money gains you nothing. Counterparty credit risk therefore exists in one direction only - and that asymmetry is exactly what makes it hard to price. Contracts are not terminated automatically on going negative, collateral flows in both directions under a normal agreement, and no accounting rule is what creates the effect.

practicePrompt.question: A bank has an interest rate swap with a company just downgraded from A to BB. The contract currently stands 5m USD in the bank's favour. What should happen to the CVA the bank books?
options: CVA should rise, because that counterparty's probability of default has risen
CVA needs no adjustment, since the contract is signed and later ratings are irrelevant
The bank should write the contract's value off its books entirely and immediately
CVA applies only to CDS contracts and never to an interest rate swap of this kind
practicePrompt.explanation: CVA has to be refreshed continuously against both the market value of the contract and the counterparty's current probability of default, usually inferred from the CDS spread where one exists. A downgrade is a direct signal to adjust CVA upward.

keyTakeaways: CVA quantifies the cost of the risk that a derivative counterparty defaults at a moment when the contract stands in your favour
CVA arises only from expected positive exposure - if you owe the counterparty, their default costs you nothing
Lehman Brothers (2008) is the direct reason Basel III added a CVA capital charge; derivative counterparty losses had sat outside the formal capital framework
A portfolio credit risk model has to account for default correlation between loans, not just individual default probabilities - the same correlation lesson the CDOs taught

summary.keyIdea: Only the positive value creates exposure - if the contract stands against you, the counterparty's default costs you nothing. That is why every CVA formula contains a max(·, 0).
summary.commonMistake: Measuring exposure on notional value. The notional figure is almost always many times larger than the real exposure.

application.title: After the exposure is measured
application.message: Most counterparty risk reduction comes from netting terms and collateral arrangements, not from the model. The model only measures what is left once those two have done their work.

sections.text: The previous two lessons covered the credit risk of a direct borrower and of a securitised pool. This one closes Credit Risk from a different angle: the credit risk hiding inside derivative contracts that most people never think of as a loan at all.

sections.title: The conceptual CVA formula
sections.label: CVA
sections.equation: CVA ≈ counterparty probability of default × (1 − recovery rate) × expected positive exposure

variables.name: Probability of default
variables.description: Inferred from the counterparty's CDS spread where one exists, or from an internal rating model

variables.name: Expected Positive Exposure
variables.description: The expected positive value of the contract at future points in time, obtained by simulation

example.title: Reading the result
example.explanation: This is the cost the bank has to book the moment the contract is signed, reflecting counterparty risk across the whole life of the trade rather than waiting for a default to occur.

sections.label: The link back to credit correlation
sections.text: At portfolio level, credit risk is not simply the sum of the individual exposures. If a bank holds 100 derivative contracts with 100 different counterparties but all of them operate in one sector - energy, say - a single oil price shock can push many of them into default at once, which is exactly the correlation-converging-in-a-crisis pattern from the Foundations stage.

lines: Credit risk does not live only with the borrower - it hides in every contract where one side can end up owing the other, including a derivative that looks purely technical.
Credit Risk Measurement and Management closes here; the next stage moves to a subject often dismissed because it carries only 10% of the exam - Current Issues in Financial Markets.
